title: Supersonic airliner in doubt as company shifts to powering AI data centers
content:
Boom Supersonic CEO Blake Scholl recently declared “it’s time for a renaissance in energy and in supersonic flight” as the supersonic airliner company unveiled a Colorado factory dedicated to making gas turbines for AI data centers. But Boom may be facing turbulence after early backers for both ventures have questioned the company’s delivery timeline or backed out entirely.
One of the company’s first customers, United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby, has expressed doubts about Boom’s original plan to deliver the first Overture supersonic airliner in 2029. Kirby’s latest frank assessment came during an interview with the Office Hours: Business Edition podcast that appeared on October 28, 2026.
“‘29 is their official timeline,” Kirby told podcast host Monica Langley. “It’s not going to happen in ‘29—it’s going to take longer.”
Boom first made headlines for flying its XB-1 demonstrator aircraft in 2024 and 2025 to demonstrate a “boomless cruise” concept that harnesses the Mach cutoff phenomenon. Such a feat involves flying just beyond supersonic speeds at higher altitudes under specific atmospheric conditions, so that the aircraft’s shockwaves refract upward and minimize the impact on the ground.
The company’s plan to revive supersonic air travel has been backed by the Trump administration via efforts to ease regulations. In June 2026, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) proposed a new rule overturning a long-standing ban on commercial supersonic flights over the United States, following an executive order from President Donald Trump.
Boom’s press releases have previously described achieving aircraft certification and carrying the first paying customers by 2029. The company has conditional agreements with American Airlines, Japan Airlines, and United Airlines involving non-refundable deposits of unknown amounts that would allow the airlines to fully purchase the Overture aircraft once it becomes commercially available.

report.summary: United’s CEO doubts Boom Supersonic will deliver its Overture jet by 2029, as Boom pivots factory capacity toward gas turbines for AI data centers.
report.background: Boom Supersonic is trying to revive commercial supersonic flight, a goal dormant since Concorde retired in 2003. Its XB-1 demonstrator flew in 2024 and 2025, testing “boomless cruise” by using Mach cutoff to refract shockwaves upward. The company has conditional deals with United, American, and Japan Airlines, and in June 2026 the FAA proposed lifting the long-standing ban on overland supersonic flights after a Trump executive order. But Boom is also building gas turbines for AI data centers in Colorado, reflecting how AI’s electricity demand has become a major industrial market. Early backers are now questioning whether Boom can meet its 2029 certification and delivery timeline.
key_points: United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby said Boom’s official 2029 timeline for delivering the first Overture supersonic airliner “is not going to happen” and will take longer. United is one of Boom’s early customers, so the public doubt carries weight beyond outside skeptics.

Boom unveiled a Colorado factory dedicated to making gas turbines for AI data centers, with CEO Blake Scholl calling it a renaissance in energy and supersonic flight. The pivot gives Boom a nearer-term revenue path but also raises questions about focus and execution.

Regulators have been moving in Boom’s favor: in June 2026 the FAA proposed overturning the ban on commercial supersonic flights over the US, following a Trump executive order. A rule change would remove a key barrier, but certification and noise concerns remain.

Boom’s airline agreements with United, American Airlines and Japan Airlines are conditional and involve non-refundable deposits of undisclosed size. They allow future purchases but do not guarantee orders, leaving Boom’s backlog vulnerable to timeline slips and regulatory delays.

The XB-1 demonstrator showed a “boomless cruise” concept using Mach cutoff and atmospheric conditions to reduce ground noise. Proving that in a small test jet is far from certifying a commercial airliner with passengers, engines and airline economics.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Boom’s turbine factory highlights how data-center power demand is pulling aerospace and energy suppliers into AI infrastructure. It could add gas-turbine capacity, but also ties AI growth to fossil-fuel generation and local emissions. For developers, the lesson is that AI scaling depends on physical power and supply chains, not just chips; energy availability may shape where models are trained and served. For regular users, supersonic travel looks further away than advertised, while AI services may keep expanding if power projects proceed. The episode also shows hype cycles colliding: a celebrated aviation startup is being judged by data-center deadlines.
report.tools: No direct open-source tool replicates Boom’s work, but readers can track the FAA’s proposed supersonic rule on Regulations.gov, watch ADS-B Exchange or OpenSky Network for XB-1 and test flights, follow Boom’s press releases, and monitor IEA and utility data-center load reports. For AI power context, compare gas-turbine announcements with data-center siting databases.
